strengths: The paper addresses an important deployment bottleneck: the visual prefix processed by the language model. Reusing encoder attention and key features makes the proposed pruning-and-merging approach simple and potentially useful, and the figures communicate the overall pipeline clearly.

PruMerge+ demonstrates a valuable accuracy–compression tradeoff across six image benchmarks and two model sizes. With 25% of the visual tokens, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2, 57.1 versus 58.2 on TextVQA, and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench (Table 1).

The Video-LLaVA experiments provide useful evidence of transfer without additional training. PruMerge improves ActivityNet-QA accuracy from 45.3 to 48.3 while substantially reducing visual tokens, although improvements are not uniform across benchmarks (Table 3).

The ablations provide evidence that informed selection and token supplementation matter. For example, training-free PruMerge achieves 54.00 on TextVQA versus 47.42 for the strongest listed spatial-sampling baseline at the same average token count (Table 4). Tables 5–6 also examine merging and fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Comparison protocols do not sufficiently isolate the method's contribution. The main image results use an additional LoRA fine-tuning epoch, but Table 7 does not establish whether ToMe, ATS, and EViT receive equivalent adaptation or specify their insertion points and reduction schedules. CrossGet results are imported from its paper. Matched adaptation protocols, including a full-token model receiving the same additional training, are needed to substantiate the reported advantages.

The central benefit of adaptive allocation remains insufficiently demonstrated. The method combines established attention-based selection, IQR thresholding, and similarity-based merging, but the ablations do not compare adaptive IQR selection against fixed top-k attention selection with the same average budget and merging procedure. Likewise, PruMerge+ needs controls that separate spatial supplementation from simply retaining more tokens. The existing experiments support informed compression more clearly than the specific adaptive design.

Efficiency validation is incomplete. Table 2 explicitly presents roofline estimates for prefill, without measured end-to-end latency or memory including reduction overhead, decoding, and variable-length batching. Additionally, the O(n) clustering claim on page 3 is unsupported by the described computation: forming KK^T requires quadratic similarity computation, and exhaustive comparison of m anchors against n tokens requires O(mn) similarities. This weakens the claimed scalability advantage over CrossGet.

Algorithm details leave material reproducibility ambiguities. Algorithm 1 adds m spatial tokens to m selected anchors, which does not explain the reported change from 5.5% retention for PruMerge to 25% for PruMerge+. Its subsequent loop and output still reference only m tokens. The neighborhood size k and attention-head aggregation are unspecified, and line 10 gives an unnormalized weighted sum although the method is described as weighted averaging. These choices directly affect the representation and computational budget.

Claims of preserving performance under aggressive compression exceed the evidence. At 5.5% retention, the 7B model drops from 78.5 to 72.0 on VQAv2, 85.9 to 76.3 on POPE, and 1510.7 to 1350.3 on MME, despite fine-tuning (Table 1). Section 4.1 also incorrectly claims improved POPE performance. The stronger 25% results support a useful tradeoff, but they do not substantiate the broader claims made for the aggressive setting.
